text:
Peas are a gut-health MVP: they bring fiber that helps keep digestion moving, plus prebiotic fibers that feed your beneficial gut bacteria. They also contain resistant starch and fermentable carbs that can support a healthier microbiome.

And here’s what makes them even more valuable—those fermentable fibers get broken down by your gut microbes into short-chain fatty acids like butyrate, which help nourish your gut lining, reduce inflammation, and support overall gut function. On top of that, peas provide plant-based protein and polyphenols that further support microbial diversity and metabolic health.

There are several factors that can lead to the opening(not completely closing) of the lower esophageal sphincter.

This is a mystery condition that actually affects more people than classic heartburn — and most don’t realize it.

If you have constant throat clearing, a sour or bitter taste in your mouth, a chronic cough, or a persistent sensation of a lump in your throat that never seems to go away, these can be signs of laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR). Unlike typical acid reflux, LPR often shows up without obvious heartburn, which is why it’s so commonly missed.

text:
Chronic throat clearing doesn’t directly cause esophageal cancer, but it can be a sign of silent acid reflux. When stomach acid repeatedly irritates the throat and esophagus, it can cause long-term inflammation and, if left untreated, increase the risk of Barrett’s esophagus, a precancerous condition. Managing reflux early helps protect your throat and esophagus.
Ways to manage acid reflux:
🍽️ Eat smaller, more frequent meals
🌶️ Avoid spicy, acidic, or fatty foods
🕐 Wait at least 2–3 hours before lying down after eating
🛏️ Elevate your head while sleeping
⚖️ Maintain a healthy weight
🚭 Avoid smoking and limit alcohol intake
💊 Talk to your doctor about medications if symptoms persist
Have you ever thought throat clearing could be linked to reflux like this?

Four days. Your gut is done waiting.

Constipation happens when stool moves too slowly through the colon and dries out. Not enough water, not enough fiber, not enough movement and your colon absorbs every bit of moisture it can find, making things painful to pass. The pressure builds. The discomfort builds. Your body starts making it very, very clear.

Drink more fluids, add fiber slowly, and stay active. If it's been more than a week or the pain is getting worse, see a doctor.
